title: Kali, Called Ma
hookLine: the fiercest face of the Goddess, and the devotees who simply call her mother
carry: god as mother: fierce, and still ma
tomorrow: kali won't stop dancing, and a god lies down in her path

lines: A DARK GODDESS ON THE KITCHEN WALL.
cards: On a kitchen wall in a family home hangs a calendar print. The goddess on it is dark blue, nearly black, her hair wild, her tongue out. She holds a sword, and a garland of severed heads hangs at her neck.
A visitor who has never seen her might take a step back. Then the grandmother of the house walks past, touches the frame, and says softly, Ma. Mother.
Nothing frightened in it at all. Today's character is Kali, and how both reactions can happen in one kitchen.

teach.h: KALI LEAPS FROM THE GODDESS'S BROW.
teach.b: In the Devi Mahatmya, which this path just read, Kali walks onto the page in battle.
The Goddess's face goes dark with anger, and from her forehead Kali leaps out: gaunt, fierce, with a sword and a noose, roaring, tearing through the enemy army.
There, she is what the Goddess's anger looks like let loose on evil. So far, terrifying. But the stories keep going.
In Bengal, poets came who didn't run from her. Tradition remembers Ramprasad Sen, who sang to Kali the way a child talks to a mother: teasing, complaining, sulking, refusing to be sent away.
In his songs she's dark and wild, still his mother, and he expects her to answer. Later, in a Kali temple near Kolkata, a priest named Ramakrishna served her image every day.
The stories say he spoke to her as Mother, longed to see her, and wept when he couldn't. Visitors found a man who talked about this fearsome goddess the way a small boy talks about his mom.
This is Shakta devotion: worshipping God as Mother. Its teaching is bold.

teach.h: A POET SINGS TO HER LIKE A CHILD.
teach.b: The power behind everything, birth and death, gentle and terrible, is a mother, and you may talk to her like her child. So here is Kali as a character.
She isn't tame; nobody in these stories pretends she's gentle, and the sword stays in her hand.
And still the people closest to her call her by a child's word for mother.
Some devotees put it this way: she is fierce toward what harms her children, and that's exactly why her children aren't afraid of her.

how: Devotees in Bengal and beyond worship Kali as Mother, singing Shakta songs to her, including ones attributed to Ramprasad Sen, and the Kali temple at Dakshineswar, where Ramakrishna served, is still a place of daily worship.

games.why: tradition remembers his songs as a child's talk with a mother: he sulks, argues and refuses to be sent away.

practice: Kali's devotees often just say her name, or simply Ma, again and again, the way Ramprasad sang it. Let something you're afraid of come to mind, not to fix it, just to see it.

Then, if you pray, say Ma softly a few times, as a child would, and let the fear sit beside her. If you don't pray, picture someone fierce on your side, and notice how the fear changes when you're not alone.

wordCard.voice: Durga. The name over this whole stretch, and the Goddess from whose brow, in the Devi Mahatmya, Kali leaps out. Today's word.
